claims.text: A nanoscale precipitate network governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion plasma-facing refractory alloys.
Dispersed nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation glide.
Precipitate-mediated obstruction of dislocations increases alloy strength.
Pinning dislocations with nanoscale precipitates enhances strain hardening.
Nanoscale precipitates act as stress concentrators that facilitate dislocation nucleation.
Nanoscale precipitates trigger alternate dislocation pathways, including cross-slip.
Alternate dislocation pathways enabled by the precipitates promote plastic deformation and improve toughness.
The dual obstacle-and-dislocation-source role of precipitates can simultaneously promote strength and ductility.
Thermal treatment can modify precipitate size and number density.
Precipitate density and size can be altered independently while grain size, composition, and dislocation density remain constant.
Temperatures above approximately 1073 K are fusion-relevant testing conditions for the proposed plasma-facing alloys.
An optimal intermediate precipitate network will increase high-temperature plastic strain relative to the conventionally processed baseline.
An optimal intermediate precipitate network will enhance toughness relative to the conventionally processed baseline.
Too few precipitates will reduce toughness because strengthening is insufficient.
An excessive precipitate population will reduce toughness by overly restricting dislocation mobility.
The hypothesized relationship is bounded to cases in which grain size, composition, and dislocation density are invariant apart from controlled precipitate changes.
The optimal precipitate density and magnitude of mechanical improvement may vary with alloy system and thermal history.
A same-base-material comparison in which only precipitate size and density vary is intended to isolate the precipitate-network effect.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes minor compositional adjustments to change precipitates while also requiring alloy composition to remain constant; the boundary and falsification design likewise require invariant composition.
